_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-15) main-session review: two board labels shortened to 18 characters or fewer

v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version. Every time comes from the sim's stated steps (0.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 0.5, 3.4 and a 0.7 first sentence) and the 23 calls' stated extra summary time (0 to 0.8 s), so earlier calls ran 8.3 to 9.1 s, under the 10 s silence limit. The line was quiet from 21:40 to 00:14, so the 22:00 change met its first call after midnight.
title: Seconds Feel Like Hours
setting: a plumber's emergency line at 2 AM

post.author: u/night_board_kalinda
post.title: I'm the night dispatcher for an emergency plumber. Our phone assistant's log says it answered all 23 callers after midnight, each with a plumber and a time. Not one of them heard a word.

blocks.text: I'm Kalinda, night dispatcher at Dobrin's, an emergency plumbing firm: burst pipes, leaks, no heat, any hour. My shift is 20:00 to 06:00. I watch the job board, the screen listing every booked job, and phone the plumbers on call.
Since spring, a voice assistant answers our line: a program that listens to the caller and talks back. Behind it is a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back.

It works in steps, and each step waits for the one before, like buckets passed hand to hand. Steps like that are called a chain. When the caller stops talking, first a speech to text program writes down what they said. Then the model checks how urgent it is. Then it writes a one-line summary of the problem. Then the app finds the nearest free plumber. Last, the model writes the whole reply, and only then does the assistant start speaking.

The assistant's log times every step. On a typical call that is 0.6 + 1.8 + 2.0 + 0.5 + 3.4 seconds: 8.3 seconds of silence before the first word. A long story takes longer to summarise; our slowest calls reached 9.1.

Our phone service hangs up any call after 10 seconds of silence, taking the line for dead. Music or talk restarts that count; only silence runs it down. The 10 seconds is a setting on our account, called the silence limit. No call had ever reached it.

At 22:00 Mr Dobrin added a third check after the summary: a gas check. The model looks for any sign of a gas smell and, if it finds one, tells the caller to leave the house. It takes 2.2 seconds. Nobody rang from 21:40 until 00:14. Then the first hard frost of the year arrived, and pipes started splitting.
Here is call 1 in the assistant's log. Each line shows the time, to a tenth of a second, and the step that finished then.

00:14:06.0  caller stops talking
00:14:06.6  speech to text done
00:14:08.4  urgency: urgent
00:14:10.4  summary: burst pipe under the kitchen sink
00:14:12.6  gas check: no gas
00:14:13.1  nearest plumber: Imrich
00:14:16.5  reply written, speaking:
            Imrich is on his way, about 35 minutes.
By 02:05 the log held 23 calls like it, every reply spoken in full, each with a plumber's name and arrival time. Each one put a job on the board, and the plumbers drove out. Nobody rang back.
At 02:10 Imrich rang me from a doorstep. The woman there said nobody had answered. She'd turned the water off herself and thought we were closed.
I asked the phone service for its own call list. All 23 calls end the same way: hung up by the line, 10.0 seconds after the caller's last word. I drew call 1 from both records.

diagram.aria: Call 1, from 00:14:06, the caller's last word, to 12 seconds later. Speech to text runs 0 to 0.6 seconds, the urgency check 0.6 to 2.4, the summary 2.4 to 4.4, the gas check 4.4 to 6.6, the plumber search 6.6 to 7.1, and the whole reply is written from 7.1 to 10.5. The caller hears silence from 0 to 10 seconds. The line hangs up at 10.0 seconds; the first word was due at 10.5.

blocks.caption: Drawn from the assistant's log and the phone service's call list. Each step starts when the one before ends: 0.6 + 1.8 + 2.0 + 2.2 + 0.5 + 3.4 = 10.5 seconds to the first word. The line hung up at 10.0, half a second before the assistant began to speak.

blocks.text: Mr Dobrin wants the gas check kept. Tomorrow night's forecast is another hard frost. What should we change before 20:00?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on your line is haunted; the assistant just never learned the caller had gone. Two times matter. Total time runs until the reply's last word is written. The wait before the first word is the one a caller lives through; this course calls it time to first token, TTFT, a token being a small piece of text a model writes (a2e07). Three questions. Which steps need another step's answer before they can start? How soon is the first sentence of a reply written? And across the 23 calls, what were the average wait and the slowest?

replies.author: u/night_board_kalinda
replies.text: The three checks each read only what speech to text wrote down. The plumber search needs the urgency and the summary, to know how soon and what kind of plumber. The reply needs everything. Mr Dobrin says a reply's first sentence is written about 0.7 seconds after the model starts it. Tonight's 23 calls waited 10.7 seconds on average; the slowest, 11.3, was a woman with a long story about her loft. Our provider, the company that runs the model, also sells a smaller model, faster and cheaper. He chose the larger one when we started.

replies.author: u/gradient_ghost
replies.text: Two words you may want. A model can send its reply in pieces as it writes, so the first sentence arrives long before the last; that is streaming (a2e07). And calls that don't need each other's answers can run at once, side by side, instead of one after another; those are parallel calls (a4e02). Whether either is worth it here is your call.

comments.author: u/hold_the_line_ekwueme
comments.text: The bug is the phone company's 10-second limit. Nobody hangs up in 10 seconds; I've sat on hold with my bank for forty minutes. Your assistant did everything right: it heard every caller, checked for gas, found a plumber and answered. The line cut it off half a second before it spoke. Set the limit to 30 and leave a working assistant alone.

replies.author: u/night_board_kalinda
replies.text: It's a setting on our account. Mr Dobrin could change it tonight.

comments.author: u/stopcock_vasquez
comments.text: I was one of your 23, at 01:44. The pipe by my boiler had split and I could smell gas. I said so. Then nothing. Ten seconds of nothing on an emergency line feels like an hour; even music would have told me someone was there. I rang the gas emergency line myself.

replies.author: u/night_board_kalinda
replies.text: You're in the log at 01:44. The gas check found it, and the reply says: leave the house now and ring the gas emergency line. It was spoken into a line that had already hung up. I'm so sorry.

reply.prompt: The frost comes back tomorrow night, and the gas check stays. What should Dobrin's change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the line's silence limit to 30 seconds, so no call is cut off while the reply is built.
options.verdict: No call cut off, the same silence
options.part2: Mr Dobrin set the silence limit to 30 seconds, and I replayed the frost night's 23 calls through it. None was cut off: every caller stayed on the line and heard the reply. But every one first sat through the same silence: 10.5 seconds on call 1, 10.7 on average, 11.3 on the slowest, the woman with the loft. The wait didn't move by a tenth of a second; we had only stopped the line from noticing it. The silence limit had been the one thing in the building measuring how long callers waited, and now it measured nothing. The next step anyone adds will make the wait longer again, with no alarm left to ring.
options.senior: The limit didn't cause the problem; it was the only thing that noticed it. A chain's wait is the sum of its steps, so every step added makes the silence longer, and raising the limit only moves the cliff. The caller still waits 10.5 seconds on an emergency line. Cut the time to the first word instead, keep the limit as a last guard, and alert well below it on the slowest calls, so the next added step is caught by you and not by a caller. OpenAI's latency guide puts it as making users wait less, and lists streaming as the single most effective approach.

options.text: Use a smaller, faster model for each check and the reply, so the chain ends inside ten seconds.
options.verdict: Under the line, and the urgent calls slip
options.part2: Mr Dobrin switched every check and the reply to the smaller model, and I replayed the 23 calls. All 23 were kept: 0.6 + 1.1 + 1.2 + 1.3 + 0.5 + 2.0 = 6.7 seconds of silence on call 1, 6.9 on average, 7.5 on the slowest. Then he read the urgency results. Of the 10 calls the larger model marked urgent, the smaller one marked 3 as can wait until morning: 00:52, 01:31 and 01:53. The one at 01:53 was water running through a ceiling light. It is still a chain, too: every step still waits for the one before, and callers still sit through more silence than they would with the steps rearranged.
options.senior: A smaller model makes each step quicker without changing the shape: the waits still add up, so the next added step eats the saving. And the steps are not all equal. OpenAI's guide says smaller models usually run faster and, when used correctly, can even outperform larger models; used correctly means tested on your own task first. Here the urgency check is the one job that must not get worse. Fix the shape first, running independent steps at once and streaming the reply, then try a smaller model one step at a time, on a step where your own test calls show no loss.

options.text: Run the three separate checks at once and start speaking at the reply's first sentence.
options.part2: Mr Dobrin changed two things. The urgency check, the summary and the gas check now start together the moment speech to text is done, and the plumber search waits only for the slowest of them, the gas check at 2.2 seconds. And the reply now streams: the assistant starts speaking at the first sentence, about 0.7 seconds in, while the rest is still being written. Replayed, call 1's first word comes at 0.6 + 2.2 + 0.5 + 0.7 = 4.0 seconds. All 23 calls are kept: 4.1 seconds on average, 4.6 on the slowest, the loft call, whose summary alone took 2.8. The whole reply is still finished at 6.7 seconds on call 1, but by then the caller has been listening for nearly 3. The gas check stays, and costs two tenths of a second: without it the summary, at 2.0, would be the slowest check. Mr Dobrin also put each night's average and slowest first word on the job board.
options.senior: Measure the wait the person feels, the time to the first word, separately from total time. Then look at the shape: in a chain the steps add up, so find the steps that don't need each other's answers and run them at once, where the wait is only the slowest of them. OpenAI's guide says it plainly: if the steps are not strictly sequential, you can split them out into parallel calls. Then stream, so speaking starts at the first sentence instead of the last; the guide calls streaming the single most effective approach. Here running the checks at once cut 3.8 seconds and streaming 2.7. Last, watch the slowest calls, not only the average: replayed without the gas check, tonight's calls average 8.5 seconds, and the slowest is already 9.1.

options.text: Play hold music from the first second, so callers know the line is alive while they wait.
options.part2: Mr Dobrin set hold music to play from the caller's last word. The phone service counts only silence, so no call was cut off: all 23 were kept. But the first word came no sooner: 10.5 seconds on call 1, 10.7 on average, 11.3 on the slowest. On an emergency line, with water coming through the ceiling, callers heard ten seconds of music before anyone spoke to them. And the silence limit could no longer see the wait at all: music fills it, so the next step added would stretch it again without a single dropped call to warn us.
options.senior: Showing the line is alive is good practice, and OpenAI's guide lists it: show your steps, and spinners and progress bars go a long way. But it is the last thing you do, after the wait is as short as you can make it, not instead. Music covers 10.5 seconds without removing one, and it also hides the signal that told you something was wrong. Cut the wait first, then fill what is left with something honest, such as a short spoken line while the checks run.

sim.title: Replay the frost night's 23 calls
sim.lede: You're Mr Dobrin, replaying the 23 calls of the first hard frost, 00:14 to 02:05, through the assistant's steps. No real model runs here: every step's time is stated, counted from the caller's last word. Larger model, as built: speech to text 0.6 s, urgency check 1.8, problem summary 2.0, gas check 2.2, nearest plumber 0.5, whole reply 3.4; with streaming, the first sentence is ready 0.7 s after the reply starts. Each call's summary takes longer when the caller talked longer: 0 to 0.8 s extra, stated per call. The smaller model takes 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 2.0 s for the checks and the reply (0.4 to the first sentence); speech to text and the plumber search are not model steps and don't change. In a chain each step waits for the one before. At once, the three checks start together and the plumber search waits for the slowest, because it needs the urgency and the summary. The phone line hangs up after the silence limit of silence; music is not silence. Of the 23 calls, the larger model marked 10 urgent; when Mr Dobrin replayed the night through the smaller model, it marked 3 of those 10 as can wait until morning. With 23 calls, the 99th percentile is the slowest call. You open at 00:00, tonight's settings in place, nothing replayed.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Replay the 23 calls and read 10.5 s to the first word, 0 of 23 kept. Turn the gas check off to see the nights before: 8.3 s, slowest 9.1. Try the 30 s limit and hold music (kept, the same wait), the smaller model (6.7 s, 3 urgent calls marked for morning), then the checks at once and streaming, each alone and together, and draw call 10. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the line was haunted. Every step waited for the one before, so the waits added up: 8.3 seconds of silence before the first word, until a 2.2-second gas check joined the chain at 22:00 and made it 10.5, past the line's 10-second silence limit. The assistant kept writing replies to callers the line had already hung up on.

steps.title: A chain adds up, step by step.
steps.text: First speech to text writes down the call: 0.6 seconds. Then the urgency check reads it: 1.8. Then the summary: 2.0. Then, since 22:00, the gas check: 2.2. Then the plumber search: 0.5. Then the whole reply: 3.4. Each starts only when the one before ends, so the caller's silence is the sum, 10.5 seconds. What can go wrong: the sum grows quietly. Each new step looks small on its own, and nobody owns the total, so the step that crosses a limit is just the last one added, here a sensible safety check.

steps.title: Time to first word against total time.
steps.text: Total time runs until the reply's last word is written. The wait a caller lives through is shorter: until the first word is spoken. For a model's reply this course calls it time to first token, TTFT (a2e07); OpenAI's latency guide doesn't use that phrase, but its principle make your users wait less is the same idea. Before tonight the two were equal, because nothing was spoken until everything was written. What can go wrong: a dashboard that shows only total time, or only the average, can look fine while callers sit in silence. Measure the first word on every call.

steps.title: Run independent steps at once.
steps.text: Ask of each step: what does it need before it can start? The urgency check, the summary and the gas check each need only the written-down call, so they can start together the moment speech to text is done; the wait for all three is then the slowest of them, 2.2 seconds, instead of their sum, 6.0. The plumber search needs the urgency and the summary, so it still waits for them. That cut alone takes call 1 from 10.5 to 6.7 seconds. What can go wrong: the work and the bill are the same, only the waiting overlaps; and a step that really needs another's answer must stay behind it, or it works from nothing.

steps.title: Stream the reply, and start speaking at the first sentence.
steps.text: First the model starts writing the reply. Second, with streaming, each piece is sent as it is written, so the first sentence is ready about 0.7 seconds in. Third, the assistant starts speaking it while the rest is still being written. Alone, streaming takes call 1 from 10.5 to 7.8 seconds; with the checks at once, to 4.0. OpenAI's guide calls streaming the single most effective approach to making users wait less, and it usually is, because the reply is usually the longest step. Here three checks in a row were longer still. What can go wrong: a sentence already spoken can't be taken back, so put anything the checks must decide, like the gas warning, before the reply starts.

steps.title: Measure the slow calls, not only the average.
steps.text: An average hides the calls that matter most. Replayed without the gas check, as the line ran before 22:00, tonight's 23 calls average 8.5 seconds, comfortably under 10, but the slowest, the loft call, takes 9.1: under a second from the cliff. A percentile says how long most calls take: the 99th percentile, p99, is the time 99 calls in 100 beat. With only 23 calls, that is simply the slowest. With the fix, the average is 4.1 and the slowest 4.6. What can go wrong: a limit set by the average breaks first for the longest stories, which on an emergency line are often the worst emergencies. Alert on the slowest well before the limit.

diagram.aria: The fix. Speech to text, 0.6 seconds, feeds three checks that run at once: the urgency check, 1.8 seconds, the problem summary, 2.0, and the gas check, 2.2, the slowest. All three feed the nearest plumber search, 0.5 seconds, which feeds the reply, streamed, with its first sentence ready 0.7 seconds after it starts. First word at 4.0 seconds.

explain.caption: Read left to right. The three checks need only the written-down call, so they start together, and the plumber search waits for the slowest, the gas check at 2.2 seconds. The reply streams, so speaking starts at its first sentence: 0.6 + 2.2 + 0.5 + 0.7 = 4.0 seconds to the first word on call 1, and 4.6 on the slowest call.

fix.title: The fix: run the independent checks at once, and speak from the first sentence
fix.text: Draw the steps and what each one needs. Start the urgency check, the summary and the gas check together as soon as speech to text is done, and let the plumber search wait for the slowest of them. Stream the reply and start speaking at its first sentence, with the gas warning, when there is one, decided before the reply starts. That takes call 1 from 10.5 seconds to 4.0, and the slowest call from 11.3 to 4.6, with the gas check kept. Keep the 10-second silence limit as a last guard. Record the time to the first word on every call, show each night's average and slowest beside each other, and raise an alert long before the slowest gets near 10 seconds, so the next step anyone adds is caught by the firm and not by a caller.

limits: Running checks at once costs the same in model calls and money; only the waiting overlaps. If the provider limits how many calls you may make at a time, each call now takes three of those slots at the same moment, and a busy night reaches the cap sooner.
Streaming only helps if the rest of the reply keeps coming at least as fast as it is spoken. On most models writing is much faster than speech, but a slow provider can leave a pause mid-sentence.
With 23 calls, the slowest call is the only reading of p99 you have, and one odd call can move it. Keep the record over many nights before setting an alert by it.

head: Plan
First word, call 1
Slowest of 23
Calls kept
Urgent calls marked for morning
rows: Tonight's calls without the gas check, as before 22:00
Tonight: gas check in the chain

explain.seniorTake: When a model feature feels slow, measure the right wait first: the time until the person sees or hears something, the time to first token, kept apart from total time. Then draw the steps and what each one needs. A chain of model calls adds up, so every step anyone adds, however sensible, makes the wait longer; steps that don't need each other's answers can run at once, and then the wait is only the slowest of them. Stream the final reply so it starts at the first sentence; that is usually the biggest single cut, because the reply is usually the longest step. A smaller model is worth testing step by step, on your own examples, where accuracy holds. Timeouts and silence limits are alarms, not the problem: raising them or covering them with music hides the wait instead of shortening it. And watch the slowest calls, p99, not only the average, with an alert well below any limit, because the long, messy requests are the ones that break first.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: seven principles for lower latency
realWorld.text: OpenAI's Latency optimization guide lists seven principles: Process tokens faster. Generate fewer tokens. Use fewer input tokens. Make fewer requests. Parallelize. Make your users wait less. Don't default to an LLM. The guide does not use the phrase time to first token; that is this course's name for the wait before the first word.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: parallelize steps that don't depend on each other
realWorld.text: Under Parallelize the guide says: Parallel processing can be powerful when performing multiple steps with an LLM. If the steps are not strictly sequential, you can split them out into parallel calls. Dobrin's three checks were not strictly sequential.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: streaming is the most effective single step
realWorld.text: Under Make your users wait less, the guide says of streaming: The single most effective approach, as it cuts the waiting time to a second or less. It also suggests showing your steps, and says spinners and progress bars go a long way, which is hold music's honest cousin.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: writing the reply is usually the slow part
realWorld.text: The guide says generating tokens is almost always the highest latency step when using an LLM, and that cutting 50% of your output tokens may cut about 50% of your latency. Here the 3.4-second reply was the longest single step.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: smaller models, used correctly
realWorld.text: Under Process tokens faster, the guide says smaller models usually run faster (and cheaper), and when used correctly can even outperform larger models. Used correctly is the condition: test the smaller model on your own task, step by step, before switching.

asked: How would you cut an LLM feature's latency?
What is time to first token?
Why measure p99 and not the average?
interview.answer: I'd start by measuring the right thing. Time to first token is how long until the first piece of the answer reaches the user; total time is until the last. Users feel the first, so I measure both, per request, and look at the slowest requests, p99 or p95, not just the average, because the average hides the long, messy requests that break first and the ones nearest any timeout. Then I draw the pipeline and what each step needs. A chain of model calls adds up, so I look for steps that don't depend on each other, like several checks that all read the same input, and run them in parallel; the wait becomes the slowest step instead of the sum. Then I stream the final answer so the user sees or hears the first sentence while the rest is written; that's usually the biggest single cut, because generating output is usually the slowest step. After that, cut tokens: shorter outputs, smaller inputs, fewer calls, and test a smaller model step by step on my own examples, keeping it only where accuracy holds. Finally I'd set an alert on p99 time to first token well below any client timeout, so the next step someone adds shows up on a dashboard before it shows up as dropped requests.

terms.def: A plumbing firm that answers at any hour for burst pipes, leaks and failed heating. Dobrin's sends plumbers on call through the night.
The person who takes jobs in and sends workers out. Kalinda is Dobrin's night dispatcher, 20:00 to 06:00.
Dobrin's screen listing every booked job, its plumber and arrival time. Each call the assistant answers puts a job on it.
A program that answers a phone line: it listens to the caller, works out a reply and speaks it.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01).
A company that runs language models and sells their use, billed by the token (a1e03).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads or writes (a1e03).
A program that writes down what a person said. Dobrin's assistant runs it first, in 0.6 seconds, after the caller stops talking.
Steps run one after another, each waiting for the one before, like buckets passed hand to hand. Its wait is the sum of its steps (a4e02's fixed chain).
The model's step that decides whether a call needs a plumber now or can wait until morning. 1.8 seconds on the larger model.
The model's one-line summary of what the caller said. 2.0 seconds, plus up to 0.8 for a long story.
The step added at 22:00: the model looks for any sign of a gas smell and, if it finds one, tells the caller to leave the house. 2.2 seconds.
A setting on Dobrin's phone service: hang up any call after this many seconds of silence, taking the line for dead. 10 seconds. Music or talk restarts the count.
How long a caller or program waits for an answer before giving up (a6e02). The silence limit is the phone line's timeout.
A cheaper, faster model from the same provider. Here it takes 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 2.0 s for the checks and reply, and marks 3 of 10 urgent calls for morning.
Receiving a model's reply in small pieces as it is written, instead of all at once at the end (a2e07). Dobrin's first sentence is ready 0.7 seconds in.
How long until the first piece of a reply arrives, also called TTFT (a2e07). The course's name; OpenAI's latency guide doesn't use it.
For a voice assistant, how long from the caller's last word until the assistant starts speaking. 10.5 seconds tonight, 4.0 with the fix.
How long until the whole reply is written. With streaming it stays the same while the time to the first word shrinks.
Model calls that don't need each other's answers, run at the same time, so the wait is the slowest of them, not the sum (a4e02's parallelization).
In this case, the three checks started together after speech to text, side by side, instead of one after another.
How long something takes to answer, the waiting part of speed. Measured here from the caller's last word.
All the waits added up and divided by how many there are. Tonight's 23 calls averaged 10.7 seconds.
A time a given share of requests beat. The 50th percentile is the middle request; the 99th beats 99 in 100.
Short for the 99th percentile: the time 99 requests in 100 beat. With only 23 calls, it is simply the slowest call.
A message sent to a person automatically when a measure crosses a line you set, such as the night's slowest first word creeping toward the silence limit.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a huge amount of text, the kind providers sell.
An AI company that runs language models and publishes a Latency optimization guide for building with them.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 9.1 covers monitoring, measuring, analysing and evaluating how well a service performs.

atWork: Look for a voice or chat assistant built as a chain of model calls with a timeout somewhere in front of it: a phone line's silence limit, a browser that gives up, an app that calls yours and stops waiting after so many seconds. It is a common pattern, and a common failure: someone adds a sensible step, a safety check, a moderation pass, a translation, and the total quietly crosses the client's timeout, so every request fails while every log says it succeeded. Ask four things. What are the steps, and which of them need another step's answer before they can start? Is the final reply streamed, so the user sees or hears something at the first sentence? What is the time to the first token, measured on every request, and what is it at p99, not only on average? And who is alerted, and at what number, before the slowest requests reach the timeout? Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015 or working toward it, clause 9.1 expects you to decide what needs monitoring and measuring and to evaluate how your service performs. For an assistant on a live line, time to the first word, with its slowest values, is the measure to keep, and deciding that in the first design is far cheaper than finding at an audit, or on a frost night, that nobody was measuring the wait.

recall.prompt: Your support chat takes about 9 seconds before anything appears. Behind it, a language model rewrites the question for search (1.5 s), then the app searches the help pages (1.2 s), then searches past tickets (1.4 s), each search using the rewritten question, then the model writes the whole answer (4.5 s) and only then shows it. How would you cut the wait users feel?

keyIdeas.idea: The two searches don't need each other, so run them at the same time; the wait becomes the slower one
Stream the answer so users see the first sentence while the rest is written
Measure the time until the first word on every request, including the slowest, not only total time

recall.model: The steps form a chain, so the waits add up: 1.5 + 1.2 + 1.4 + 4.5 is 8.6 seconds before anything shows. The rewrite has to come first, but the two searches each need only the rewritten question, so I'd run them at once; their wait becomes the slower one, 1.4 instead of 2.6. Then I'd stream the answer so users see the first sentence while the rest is being written, which usually is the biggest single cut, since writing is the longest step. Finally I'd measure the time to first token, until the first word appears, on every request and watch the slowest ones, p99, not only the average or the total time.

recall.prompt: After the caller stops talking: speech to text 0.6 s; three checks that each need only the written-down call, 1.8, 2.0 and 2.2 s; a plumber search 0.5 s; then a reply whose first sentence is ready 0.7 s after it starts. With the checks run at once and the reply streamed, when is the first word spoken?
recall.why: At once, the three checks take as long as the slowest, 2.2 s. Then 0.6 + 2.2 + 0.5 + 0.7 = 4.0 s. 10.5 s is the chain without streaming, 7.8 s the chain with streaming, and 6.7 s the checks at once without streaming.

recall.prompt: Your dashboard shows the assistant's mean reply time is 3 seconds, far under the 8-second limit of the app that calls it. Yet a few users a day get a timeout error. What is going on, and what would you measure and watch instead?

keyIdeas.idea: A mean hides the slow requests; a few take far longer than the typical one
Measure a high percentile such as p99, not only the average
Alert on that slow end well before it reaches the limit

recall.model: The average hides the slow requests. Most answers take about 3 seconds, but a few, the long questions or a slow moment at the provider, take far longer, and those few cross the 8-second limit. They are the slowest one or two in a hundred, which an average barely moves. I'd measure a high percentile, p99 and p95, of the time to the first token and of total time, per request, and set an alert well below the limit on p99, so I see the slow end creeping up before users see errors.

recall.prompt: Why did Dobrin's assistant log 23 replies spoken in full when no caller heard a word?
options: The phone service's call list recorded the calls wrongly
The provider's model was down from 22:00
The steps kept running after the line hung up at 10 seconds, and nothing told them the caller had gone
The gas check stopped every reply before it was spoken
recall.why: Every call's first word was due at 10.5 seconds or later, and the line hangs up after 10 seconds of silence. The assistant never checked whether the line was still open, so it finished each reply and spoke it into a dead line.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. All winter the first word has come in about 4 seconds, and the board shows each night's average and longest wait. Now Mr Dobrin wants two more steps. A language check, 0.9 seconds, spots callers who aren't speaking English and needs only the written-down call. An address check, 1.5 seconds, confirms the street, and can only start once the problem summary has picked the street out of the call.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Where should each new step go, and what happens to the first word on a typical call?

keyIdeas.idea: The language check needs only the written-down call, so it joins the checks running at once and adds no time
The address check depends on the summary, so it lengthens that branch to 3.5 seconds, slower than the gas check
The first word moves to about 5.3 seconds; keep watching the slowest call against the limit

coldCase.model: The language check needs only the written-down call, so it starts with the other checks after speech to text; at 0.9 seconds it is faster than the gas check's 2.2, so it adds no time at all. The address check depends on the summary, so it has to run after the summary: that branch becomes 2.0 + 1.5 = 3.5 seconds, longer than the gas check, and it is now the slowest branch. A typical call's first word moves from 4.0 to 0.6 + 3.5 + 0.5 + 0.7 = 5.3 seconds, and the loft-length calls to about 6.1. Still well under 10, but it is the kind of creep that broke the frost night, so add it knowingly, keep the alert on the slowest call, and check whether the plumber search really needs the address or could start alongside it.
